approachQuestion.prompt:
A telemetry batch contains n nonnegative identifiers. Exactly one identifier occurs once, and every other identifier occurs exactly twice. Return the identifier that occurs once. The input array must remain unchanged.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; n is odd; each identifier is an unsigned 32-bit word in [0, 2^32 - 1]. The result is one unsigned 32-bit word.

Example 1: [12, 7, 12, 9, 7] -> 9.
Example 2 (edge case): [0] -> 0.
Example 3: [5, 5, 0, 0, 4294967295] -> 4294967295. Every listed identifier except the returned one appears twice.
constraints: The input values are unsigned 32-bit words; bitwise XOR is applied to all 32 bits.
The input is not modified. Hash-map operations, if used, have expected constant-time lookup/update.
Return the sole identifier with odd multiplicity; the guarantee says every other identifier occurs exactly twice.

options.text: Start with the all-zero word and XOR each identifier into it once, from left to right.
options.feedback: A value paired with itself contributes zero, so the pairs disappear and the sole unpaired identifier remains.

options.text: Count each identifier in a hash map, then return the key whose count is one.
options.feedback: This returns the right value for every allowed input and finds the unique count, but retains a table even though paired values can cancel during one pass.

options.text: Sort a copy of the values, then scan adjacent entries to find the identifier without a matching neighbor.
options.feedback: This returns the right identifier for every allowed input, but sorting a copy adds a comparison sort and extra storage that the cancellation property avoids.
The first element may be part of a pair. In [8, 3, 8], this returns 8 although the identifier occurring once is 3.

feedback.reason: Equal pairs cancel under XOR regardless of order, and zero is the identity.
details: Keep one 32-bit accumulator initialized to zero. For each identifier, combine it with the accumulator using XOR. Equal pairs cancel regardless of their positions; after the scan, only the identifier with odd multiplicity remains.

Equal pairs cancel under XOR regardless of order, and zero is the identity. The promised multiplicities leave exactly one unmatched value. If another value had odd multiplicity, the accumulator would be their XOR rather than either value.
“Start with the all-zero word and XOR each identifier into it once, from left to right.”: A value paired with itself contributes zero, so the pairs disappear and the sole unpaired identifier remains.

“Count each identifier in a hash map, then return the key whose count is one.”: This returns the right value for every allowed input and finds the unique count, but retains a table even though paired values can cancel during one pass.

“Sort a copy of the values, then scan adjacent entries to find the identifier without a matching neighbor.”: This returns the right identifier for every allowed input, but sorting a copy adds a comparison sort and extra storage that the cancellation property avoids.
“Return the first array element.”: The first element may be part of a pair. In [8, 3, 8], this returns 8 although the identifier occurring once is 3.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For xor-all-identifiers, choose the tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the number of identifiers. The input and returned word are excluded from auxiliary space.
constraints: The input values are unsigned 32-bit words; bitwise XOR is applied to all 32 bits.
The input is not modified. Hash-map operations, if used, have expected constant-time lookup/update.
Return the sole identifier with odd multiplicity; the guarantee says every other identifier occurs exactly twice.

feedback.reason: One XOR per identifier uses a fixed-width accumulator.
details: Every identifier must be inspected in the worst case, and the method retains only the 32-bit accumulator and loop state. The input is read in place; no table or copy is created.
A scan performs one fixed-width word operation per identifier. Any unread position could be the unique value, so the worst case requires inspecting all n inputs.
The accumulator and index use a fixed number of words independent of n; the supplied array and scalar output are excluded.
Unsigned 32-bit word-RAM model. XOR on one word costs O(1); no recursion or input copy is used.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This describes the map-based alternative, which allocates up to O(n) entries.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is looser than the single pass and does not describe the fixed method.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The input scan cannot be skipped in the worst case.
